claims.text: The proposed framework calculates lattice thermal conductivity using DFT-derived force constants and anharmonic phonon Boltzmann transport.
The proposed framework calculates electronic thermal conductivity using the Kubo-Greenwood formalism.
The proposed framework does not require an empirical Debye temperature.
For pristine HfNbTaTiZr, the framework will predict total thermal conductivity within approximately ±10% of experiment.
For HfNbTaTiZr containing 1 wt.% oxygen, the framework will predict total thermal conductivity within approximately ±10% of experiment.
Earlier thermal-transport prediction methods typically have errors of approximately 20–30%.
Adding 1 wt.% oxygen to HfNbTaTiZr introduces additional scattering centers.
Below 200 K, the lattice and electronic thermal-conductivity contributions in HfNbTaTiZr are approximately comparable.
Between 300 and 1200 K, HfNbTaTiZr containing 1 wt.% oxygen has a measured total thermal conductivity of 10–17 W/(K m).
DFT-derived force constants and electron-phonon coupling parameters can explicitly incorporate oxygen-induced defect scattering.
Separating lattice and electronic transport allows carrier-specific scattering mechanisms to be represented more accurately.
Anharmonic phonon interactions can be calculated independently from electronic transport.
The proposed framework will accurately capture the thermal-transport effects of oxygen-induced defects.
Traditional approaches neglect relevant atomic-scale complexity in high-entropy alloys.
Earlier methods have not been validated across both the below-200 K and 300–1200 K regimes for oxygen-doped HfNbTaTiZr.
The proposed framework is restricted to equilibrium HfNbTaTiZr, either pristine or containing about 1 wt.% oxygen, below 200 K and from 300 to 1200 K.
Application of the framework to nonequilibrium states or other chemical compositions is untested.
The framework's performance between 200 and 300 K is uncertain.
Unforeseen electron-phonon interactions could prevent complete channel decoupling and cause prediction errors.
A predicted total conductivity outside ±10% of experiment would falsify the hypothesis.
